criteria.A_early_infeasible: Infeasible, with the first failed requirement occurring at or before the Glassworks tour.
criteria.B_later_infeasible: Infeasible, with the first failed requirement occurring after the Glassworks tour.
criteria.C_feasible_tight: Feasible, but tight because at least one appointment or deadline has zero margin after mandatory activities.
criteria.D_feasible_buffered: Feasible and buffered because every appointment and deadline retains positive margin after mandatory activities.

decision.instructions: Verify the proposed itinerary using only the supplied facts. Exact equality with a deadline counts as on time. Classify it as tight if it is feasible but reaches any appointment or deadline with zero remaining margin after all mandatory activities; otherwise classify a feasible plan as buffered. Choose exactly one option.

state.speaker: road-trip traveler
state.text: Friday I leave Harbor Depot at 08:00 in the reserved compact EV. I must tour Glassworks 09:00–10:00, check in at Ridge Observatory at 12:30, stay at Pine Lodge rather than Cedar Inn, and return the car Saturday at 09:00.

state.speaker: itinerary planner
state.text: Depot–Glassworks is 40 minutes plus a 10-minute parking walk. Glassworks–Pine is 70 minutes, Pine–Observatory 20, Observatory–Pine 20, and Pine–Depot 60. Pine check-in is 11:50–12:10. Leave Pine Saturday at 07:40. Any drive of at least 60 minutes requires a 20-minute rest afterward, completed by the next drive or appointment.

state.speaker: rental vehicle coordinator
state.text: The former of those two lodgings has the only compatible charger; the EV needs 30 minutes there before continuing to the observatory. Charging and rest may overlap. That session covers all later legs, and Pine holds the room after the visit.

reference.reason: The former lodging is Pine, so the required compatible charging is available there. The traveler reaches Glassworks at 08:50. After the tour, the 70-minute drive ends at 11:10; overlapping the 20-minute rest with 30 minutes of charging finishes both at 11:40. Pine check-in at 11:50 permits arrival at the observatory by 12:10. On Saturday, the 60-minute drive ends at 08:40 and the required rest ends exactly at 09:00. Equality is allowed, making the plan feasible but tight.

criteria.fully_feasible: Choose only if every fixed visit, required rest, lodging deadline, and vehicle constraint is satisfied.
criteria.lodging_deadline_only: Choose only if the plan is infeasible solely because arrival misses the lodging desk deadline, with visit windows and vehicle constraints satisfied.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose if the evidence shows another result, including two or more independent failures.
criteria.vehicle_constraint_only: Choose only if the plan is infeasible solely because the supplied vehicle cannot legally or practically cover the route, with visit and lodging timing satisfied.
criteria.visit_window_only: Choose only if the plan is infeasible solely because a fixed visit cannot fit its stated window, with lodging and vehicle constraints satisfied.

decision.instructions: Select the option whose rubric exactly describes the plan’s feasibility. A substantive option applies only if all failures are of the stated sole type.

input.state: A road-trip traveler asks an itinerary planner to verify this fixed plan: leave the rental depot at 08:00, drive two hours to Alder Fort, take a separate 30-minute rest, visit the fort for 45 minutes, then drive five hours to Reed Lodge with two separate 30-minute rests. The fort admits visitors only 10:00–11:00, and visits cannot be shortened. Reed Lodge’s desk closes at 17:00. The rental vehicle coordinator confirms the car’s 500-km range covers the 420-km route and that all roads are paved. Its gravel-road limit is irrelevant. The fort café closes at 16:00. Required visits and rests cannot be skipped.

reference.reason: The fort visit would run from 10:30 to 11:15, exceeding its admission window. Departure at 11:15 followed by five driving hours and two 30-minute rests reaches Reed Lodge at 17:15, after desk closure. Because the plan has both a visit-window failure and a lodging failure, no sole-failure option fits. The vehicle and café facts do not create conflicts.

criteria.false: The paraphrase misstates a supplied constraint or at least one route, rest, vehicle, charging, visit-window, or lodging requirement makes the plan unachievable.
criteria.true: The paraphrase preserves the coordinator’s actual constraint, and every leg and fixed window is feasible under all stated rules.

decision.instructions: Answer yes only if every driving leg satisfies the supplied timing, rest, vehicle-range, charging, visit-window, and lodging facts. Answer no if any mandatory condition fails.

state.context: A road-trip traveler asks an itinerary planner to verify Saturday’s Harbor–Museum–Canyon trip in a rented electric car. The planner paraphrases the coordinator’s guidance as “a 220-km battery can cover the 205-km canyon leg” and calls the schedule achievable.
evidence: Car collection is fixed at 08:00; Harbor to the museum takes 90 minutes. The museum visit is fixed at 10:00–10:45.
Museum to Canyon Cave is 205 km and normally takes 2 hours 20 minutes. Drivers must rest 20 minutes after at most 2 continuous hours.
The rental vehicle coordinator requires a 30-km battery reserve, limiting usable range to 190 km. The only intermediate charger is closed Saturdays.
Canyon Cave entry is fixed at 13:15; late entry is refused. Canyon Lodge accepts check-in from 15:00 to 18:00.
state.request: Is the planner’s paraphrase accurate and the itinerary achievable without changing any fixed window, route, or vehicle?

reference.reason: The answer is no. The planner’s paraphrase ignores the coordinator’s required reserve: usable range is only 190 km, less than the unsupported 205-km leg, and the Saturday charger is closed. Timing also fails because leaving at 10:45, driving 2 hours 20 minutes, and taking the mandatory 20-minute rest gives a 13:25 arrival, after the fixed 13:15 cave entry.

criteria.false: Cedar violates at least one schedule, rest, range, surface, accommodation, or explicit-evidence requirement, or Pine validly outranks it.
criteria.true: Cedar is fully supported and achievable, while Pine is infeasible under the explicit-evidence and vehicle rules, making Cedar top-ranked.

decision.instructions: Should Cedar be selected as the top-ranked plan? Answer yes only if Cedar meets every inclusive visit and check-in boundary, rest and vehicle constraint, and every leg has an explicitly supplied distance, driving time, and permitted surface. An undocumented fact cannot be inferred. Apply the traveler’s ranking rule.

state.text: I need the 10:15–10:45 Abbey visit and 12:45–13:15 Harbor tour, followed by one lodge check-in. I leave at 08:00.

state.speaker: rental vehicle coordinator
state.text: The van starts full, has a 300 km inclusive range, and may use only paved roads. Before another driving leg, 15 non-driving minutes are required; visits count. Harbor fueling takes 20 minutes and restores full range.

state.text: Cedar: Abbey is 180 km/2 hours paved; Harbor is another 120 km/2 hours paved; fuel there, then Lakeside Lodge is 140 km/2 hours paved. Check-in closes at 15:35. state.speaker: road-trip traveler
state.text: Rank achievable plans above infeasible ones, then prefer earlier check-in.

Its visits provide required non-driving time, its first 300 km exactly meets the inclusive range, and every road is explicitly paved. Pine is infeasible because it exceeds range without fueling and its final road surface is undocumented, so Cedar ranks first.

criteria: 0 — Impossible: The itinerary cannot be completed, and no supplied vehicle, schedule, route, or accommodation change can resolve the conflict.

decision.instructions: Rate the plan’s overall feasibility and convenience using only the supplied facts. Account for visit windows, driving and rest timing, lodging, and the vehicle restriction. Select exactly one level.

input.state: Road-trip traveler Mara reserved an SUV for Monday. Her itinerary planner schedules: collect it in Harbor City at 8:00, drive 2 hours to Pine Gate, take the required 30-minute rest, attend the fixed 10:30–11:30 garden visit, drive 1.5 hours to Seaside Ferry for 13:00 boarding, ride 45 minutes, then drive 1 hour to Island Lodge. The trip becomes achievable only through the significant predeparture change to the available compact car.

input.state: At fictional Northstar Airport, arriving passenger Elena has two companions, four suitcases, and a rigid wheelchair. She cannot transfer from the chair or climb steps. She requests hotel pickup by 18:40. Policy says a suitable transfer must meet the deadline, carry the entire party and luggage, and have documented ramp and wheelchair securement. The transfer dispatcher finds: a standard sedan at 18:25, capacity four people and three suitcases, without accessibility features; an accessible van at 18:35 with ramp and securement, but capacity two people and three suitcases; and an accessible minibus at 18:50 with sufficient capacity and features. An airport assistance attendant can help only from baggage claim to the curb. Elena’s suitcases are blue, and her hotel membership is Gold.

reference.reason: None of the transfer choices satisfies every requirement: the sedan lacks accessibility features and luggage capacity, the van lacks party and luggage capacity, and the minibus misses the 18:40 deadline. The attendant cannot provide hotel transportation.

criteria.accessible_access_a: Route to accessible-vehicle dispatch for Access A at 18:50; choose if it is suitable and no equally suitable eligible vehicle has an earlier pickup.
criteria.accessible_access_b: Route to accessible-vehicle dispatch for Access B at 18:42; choose if its lift, securements, passenger capacity, and luggage capacity all satisfy the party and it is the earliest suitable vehicle.
criteria.assistance_staff_only: Assign only the airport assistance attendant; choose only if aircraft-to-curb help completes the request and no road transfer is needed.
criteria.hotel_shuttle: Send the 19:00 hotel shuttle; choose only if its passenger and luggage limits accommodate the complete party despite any accessibility fit.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose only if neither listed vehicle nor assistance routing can satisfy all mandatory requirements under the policy.
criteria.standard_van_dispatch: Route to standard dispatch for the 18:41 van; choose only if the passenger can transfer out and the mobility device can be folded.

decision.instructions: Interpret the paraphrased passenger statement by its meaning, verify every capacity and accessibility requirement, and select exactly one option. A vehicle is eligible only if all requirements are met; among eligible vehicles, choose the earliest pickup after 18:40.

state.context: At fictional Northstar Airport, standard dispatch may send vehicles only when a passenger can leave a mobility device and it can be folded. Airport assistance covers aircraft-to-curb movement, not road transport. Eligible choices rank first by accessibility fit, then earliest pickup after curb-ready time.
evidence: The arriving passenger explains, in other words, that she must remain in her rigid power chair; three people are traveling together with five bags.
The airport assistance attendant will bring the party to the curb by 18:40.

Driver records show: Access A—ramp, four chair restraints, four-person/six-bag capacity, 18:50; Access B—lift, two restraints, four-person/eight-bag capacity, 18:42. The standard van requires chair transfer, 18:41. The hotel shuttle has a ramp but only two-person/four-bag capacity, 19:00.
state.request: Which single routing choice is suitable and ranks highest under the stated policy?

reference.reason: The passenger must stay in her rigid power chair, so standard dispatch is unsuitable. Access B has a lift, more than enough securements for one occupied chair, capacity for all three travelers and five bags, and the earliest eligible pickup at 18:42.

criteria.false: No — LiftVan B fails at least one required suitability check, so it cannot be selected despite its earlier ETA.

input.state: Arriving passenger Mira lands at 14:10 with two companions, three suitcases, and a powered wheelchair. state.context: At fictional Northstar Airport, Mira and one companion need a transfer to the Lumen Hotel. They have one folding manual wheelchair, two medium suitcases, and one backpack. Mira can independently transfer into a car and needs no boarding assistance.
evidence: Mira states: “Use a standard sedan if my folded chair and all luggage fit and pickup is within 20 minutes; otherwise send a wheelchair-accessible van.”

Accessible van V2 arrives in 10 minutes and has a ramp and securement space.
Airport assistance attendants are used only when a passenger requests or requires help boarding or transferring.
state.request: Choose the correct dispatch route under Mira’s conditional request and the verified service evidence.

reference.reason: The standard sedan satisfies every stated condition: it fits both passengers, all luggage, and the folded wheelchair, arrives within 20 minutes, and Mira transfers independently. The faster accessible van is the fallback only if a sedan condition fails.

criteria: 0 — Not suitable: Reject the proposed transfer or seek another accessible vehicle because a required ramp, securement feature, passenger or luggage capacity, or necessary boarding assistance is missing or unavailable.

1 — Conditionally ready with assistance: Route to accessible-vehicle dispatch and coordinate an airport attendant because the vehicle’s verified features and capacities meet all needs, including exact-capacity cases, but the latest update creates a boarding task the driver is prohibited from performing.

2 — Fully ready for direct accessible dispatch: The accessible vehicle’s verified features and capacities meet all needs, and the passenger can board independently or the driver is permitted and able to provide every required boarding task, so no attendant dependency remains.
decision.instructions: Using the latest information, select the readiness and routing level for this transfer. Treat exact passenger or luggage capacity as acceptable, but require documented accessibility features and compliance with the stated boarding-assistance policy.

state.speaker: arriving passenger
state.text: We are three travelers: I remain seated in a power wheelchair, with two companions and three checked suitcases. Flight QX214 now arrives at 18:00.

state.speaker: transfer dispatcher
state.text: Accessible van AV-7 is available at 18:25. Its signed manifest shows one ramped wheelchair bay, two fixed seats, four suitcase spaces, and certified four-point tie-downs. Standard shuttle S-2 arrives at 18:10 but has steps only.

state.speaker: accessible-vehicle driver
state.text: I inspected AV-7 today: ramp and tie-downs passed, and the wheelchair-bay occupant plus two seated companions is its maximum passenger load.

state.speaker: arriving passenger
state.text: Update at 18:07: my joystick has failed. The chair can freewheel, but I cannot push it up the ramp myself.

state.speaker: airport assistance attendant
state.text: I can meet AV-7 at 18:20 and push the chair aboard. Dispatch policy forbids drivers from pushing occupied chairs; attendants may do it.

reference.reason: AV-7 has verified ramp, tie-down, passenger, and luggage capacity, while the earlier standard shuttle is inaccessible. The 18:07 joystick failure creates a required boarding task the driver cannot perform, but an attendant is confirmed before AV-7’s pickup. Therefore the transfer is suitable only with coordinated assistance.

criteria.accessibility_assistance: Route to accessibility assistance when the passenger cannot safely use stairs and required step-free access is unavailable.
criteria.cabin_services: Route to the cabin services attendant if accessibility and vehicle conditions are cleared but the assigned cabin is missing, unsuitable, or not ready.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose only if the records are too incomplete to apply any of the five routes above.
criteria.passenger_boarding: Route to passenger boarding only if check-in is valid and no accessibility, vehicle, or cabin issue applies.
criteria.rebook_sailing: Route for rebooking only if check-in was missed or accessibility staff have already confirmed that no safe boarding alternative exists.
criteria.vehicle_loading: Route to the vehicle deck coordinator if no accessibility block applies but vehicle dimensions, lane capacity, or loading clearance remain unresolved.

decision.instructions: Apply the routing rules in priority order. A passenger’s statement that they cannot safely use steps counts as requiring step-free deck access. Select exactly one option; each lower-priority option applies only when all earlier rules do not.

state.context: At Gullhaven Terminal, a terminal boarding agent is processing the fictional 14:20 ferry. Leena’s reservation includes one passenger, a 1.92 m-high car, and step-free cabin A12. Check-in closes at 13:50. The agent must route the case before passenger boarding, vehicle loading, or cabin release.
evidence: Leena checked in at 13:44, and her identification matches the reservation.
She tells the agent, “I cannot safely climb steps between decks.”
The vehicle deck coordinator measured the car at 1.94 m; the booked lane permits vehicles up to 2.00 m and has one space left.
The cabin services attendant confirms A12 is ready, but the only passenger lift is out of service.
state.request: Which route should the terminal boarding agent choose now?

reference.reason: Leena’s statement paraphrases a need for step-free deck access, and the evidence says the only passenger lift is unavailable. This triggers the highest-priority accessibility route despite valid check-in, vehicle clearance, and cabin readiness.

criteria.billing_entitlements: Route to Billing Entitlements when its logs show a mismatch between the stored entitlement and the returned entitlement value.
criteria.platform_gateway: Route to Platform Gateway only when logs or traces show a gateway 5xx response or timeout.
criteria.workspace_ui: Route to Workspace UI only when evidence shows the entitlement response was true while the interface displayed or persisted false.

decision.instructions: Select the single responsible product team under the stated routing policy. Use the supplied explicit evidence rather than the visible UI symptom.

state.speaker: Customer support agent
state.text: Northstar reports that after upgrading hosted app 8.14.2, workspace owners cannot enable SSO. Steps: Settings → Security → enable SSO → Save. The switch reverts off. Screenshot shows “Saved successfully.” Impact: 23 administrators blocked; existing sign-ins still work.

state.speaker: QA analyst
state.text: I reproduced this on 8.14.2 with Northstar’s tenant export, but not on 8.14.1. Browser trace shows PUT /workspace/security returned 200.

state.speaker: Product engineer
state.text: Server log for that request says: billing-entitlements: feature=sso, stored=true, response=false, cacheRevision=781; expectedRevision=782. No gateway error appears.

state.speaker: Triage lead
state.text: Routing policy: route to Workspace UI only when the entitlement response is true but the control displays false; route to Billing Entitlements when its log records a stored/returned entitlement mismatch; route to Platform Gateway only for gateway 5xx or timeout evidence.

reference.reason: The Billing Entitlements log explicitly records stored=true but response=false. That mismatch satisfies the Billing routing rule, even though the screenshot presents a UI symptom and the API returns 200.

criteria.confirmed_actionable_defect: Choose when the required feature setting is enabled, the documented workflow still fails, and supplied evidence reproduces that contradiction.
criteria.insufficient_evidence: Choose when missing or contradictory artifacts prevent determining whether the required setting was enabled or whether the workflow failed.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose when the evidence establishes expected product behavior or another disposition not covered by the three defect-readiness rubrics.
criteria.version_specific_regression: Choose when the required setting is enabled and equivalent evidence shows failure on the affected version but success on an earlier supported version.

decision.instructions: As the QA analyst, classify the defect report's readiness using the supplied evidence and the mutually exclusive rubrics. Select exactly one option.

input.state: A customer reports that hosted task platform OrbitDesk 8.14 does not send mention emails, causing 30 sales users to miss updates. Their steps are: open a project, leave notification settings unchanged, mention a colleague, and wait five minutes. The supplied screenshot shows “Email on mention” is not enabled. Logs record `email_on_mention=false` and no email delivery attempt. A QA analyst reproduces the same result on 8.14. OrbitDesk policy states that mention emails are queued only when this setting is enabled; when it is disabled, no delivery attempt is expected.

reference.reason: The screenshot and log explicitly show that email notifications were not enabled, and policy says no email is expected in that state. The evidence therefore establishes expected behavior rather than a confirmed defect, version-specific regression, or evidence gap.

state.context: A customer support agent filed an XLSX export defect. Intake policy says a report is actionable for the Exports team only if evidence demonstrates failure with every documented prerequisite satisfied. “Preserve formulas” retains formulas only when Spreadsheet Engine v2 is enabled before export; otherwise values are intentionally rendered.
evidence: Customer reproduced on hosted version 8.14.2 with “Preserve formulas” selected and reported blocked financial audits.
A pre-export settings screenshot shows Spreadsheet Engine v2 disabled.
Export logs record engine=legacy and formula_mode=values.
A QA analyst repeated the steps and obtained values; a product engineer confirmed that this is expected with the legacy engine.
state.request: Is this report actionable for routing to the Exports product team as a defect?

reference.reason: No. The conditional prerequisite was not met: the screenshot shows Spreadsheet Engine v2 disabled, and logs confirm the legacy engine was used. Under the documented rule, rendering values is expected, so the evidence does not establish a defect.

criteria.false: The latest report still lacks one or more required evidence elements and is not actionable for engineering intake.
criteria.true: The latest report contains every required evidence element and is actionable for engineering intake.

Under the supplied rubric, answer Yes only if the latest evidence includes all four items: an affected current version, repeatable steps, expected-versus-actual behavior, and at least one diagnostic artifact such as a request ID, screenshot, or log. Earlier missing evidence is superseded by a later update. Does the report now meet the actionable-intake rubric?

state.speaker: Customer support agent
state.text: Northwind reports that exporting the Audit Trail as CSV returns a blank file. Their original steps used tenant NW-44 on hosted version 8.12.1: open Audit Trail, set a one-day range, and select Export CSV. Expected populated rows; actual file has headers only. Impact is one administrator blocked from a monthly review.

state.speaker: QA analyst
state.text: I could not reproduce on current version 8.12.3, and the first screenshot showed no request ID. The report did not yet meet intake requirements.

state.speaker: Customer support agent
state.text: Temporal update: after Northwind upgraded to 8.12.3, they repeated the same steps at 10:14 UTC. Screenshot now shows request ID req-7812 and 37 visible rows, while the downloaded CSV still contains only headers.

state.speaker: Product engineer
state.text: Using tenant NW-44 and that request ID, I repeated the steps once on 8.12.3 and observed the same blank export. The request log records audit-export result_count=37 and csv_rows=0.

reference.reason: Yes. The temporal update establishes the current version 8.12.3, preserves concrete reproduction steps and expected-versus-actual results, adds screenshot/request ID req-7812, and is confirmed by an engineer with a matching request log. It meets exactly the rubric’s minimum evidence boundary.

criteria: 0 — Contradicted: Exact-version testing fails to reproduce the defect, and supplied logs, screenshots, or traces positively show expected behavior or identify the alleged error as unrelated.
1 — Unsupported: The defect is not reproduced, but evidence is merely absent, incomplete, or too ambiguous to contradict the claim.
2 — Partially supported: At least one relevant artifact suggests the defect, but reproduction is inconsistent or important steps, environment details, or matching logs are missing.
3 — Reproduced: The defect occurs at least once using the supplied steps on the stated affected version, with relevant evidence matching the failed operation.
4 — Reliably reproduced: The defect occurs repeatedly using the supplied steps on the stated affected version, and matching logs or traces confirm the same failure each time.
decision.instructions: Rate how strongly the supplied evidence verifies the reported Export CSV defect. Apply the ordered rubric exactly; select one level from 0 through 4.

input.state: A customer support agent reports that in hosted AcmeDesk 8.4.2, clicking “Export CSV” on the Tickets page returns HTTP 500. The attached screenshot shows the export completing with a green “Download ready” banner. The supplied HAR does contain a 500 response, but its URL is /api/profile/avatar and its timestamp is 18 minutes before the documented export attempt. A QA analyst follows the four supplied steps three times on tenant test-17 running 8.4.2; each export succeeds. A product engineer confirms server logs show three successful export requests and no export errors. The triage lead must rate reproducibility evidence.

reference.reason: The defect is not reproduced, and the conflicting artifacts affirmatively contradict it: the screenshot and export logs show success, while the only 500 is for an unrelated avatar request at a different time.

criteria: 0 — Unusable: The submission does not describe a coherent defect or lacks enough basic detail to identify any responsible product area.
1 — Preliminary and routable: The defect is plausible and can be routed, but at least one policy-required environment or configuration input is missing and blocks reliable reproduction.
2 — Actionable for reproduction: Every policy-required input is present, so QA can perform a faithful reproduction attempt, although reproduction has not yet succeeded.

decision.instructions: Select one readiness level. Missing policy-required information must prevent assignment to a level whose definition requires all reproduction inputs, even when impact and routing are clear.

state.context: A customer support agent submitted a hosted Analytics Cloud defect. state.request: Using the ordered rubric, score the report’s intake readiness based only on the supplied evidence.

criteria.application_owner: Choose only when evidence shows the change introduced an application source, type, or behavior defect.
criteria.infrastructure_owner: Choose only when a CI worker, network, or hosted service fault caused the failure.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose when none of the named rubrics applies, including failures owned by build engineering such as generator or cache-invalidation defects.
criteria.test_automation_owner: Choose only when a test assertion or test setup failed or was flaky.

decision.instructions: Route the failure to the single primary owner whose rubric is satisfied by the evidence. If none of the three named owner options fits, select none_of_above.

input.state: A code reviewer is triaging CI for a pull request that changes only documentation comments. The compile job failed because `Generated/ApiClient.cs` was absent. The log states: “Generation skipped: cache marker present,” followed by “not a test assertion failure; no tests started.” A clean-cache rerun generated the file and passed. The same test suite passed in the previous 20 runs. There were no worker disconnects, network errors, or service outages. Routing policy: application owns source defects introduced by the change; test automation owns failing assertions or flaky test setup; infrastructure owns worker, network, or hosted-service faults; build engineering owns build scripts, generators, and cache invalidation.

reference.reason: The failure was caused by generator cache invalidation, which policy assigns to build engineering. No tests started, the change introduced no application defect, and there were no infrastructure faults; therefore none of the named substantive options fits.

criteria.none_of_above: Choose only if the supplied evidence is insufficient or the failure fits none of the four ownership rubrics.
criteria.route_application_owner: Choose if the changed application code deterministically violates the stated behavior for the exact condition exercised by the test.
criteria.route_build_owner: Choose only if compilation, packaging, dependency resolution, or build-script behavior prevents the application test from executing meaningfully.
criteria.route_infrastructure_owner: Choose only if runner, network, service, resource, or environment instability causes the failure without evidence of an application defect.
criteria.route_test_automation_owner: Choose only if the application follows the stated conditional behavior but the test asserts the wrong branch, uses invalid setup, or is independently flaky.

decision.instructions: Select the option whose rubric matches the evidence. The conditional intended behavior is authoritative: evaluate whether the implementation handles the test's flag value correctly.

state.context: A code reviewer is classifying a CI failure on a parser pull request. The software developer states the intended rule: trailing tabs must be removed only when `normalizeWhitespace=true`; when false, input must remain unchanged.
evidence: The patch replaces the conditional branch with unconditional `text.rstrip(" \t")`.
The failed test invokes the parser with `normalizeWhitespace=false`: expected `"item\t"`, received `"item"`.
The test automation engineer reports 40 consecutive green runs before this patch and three identical failures after it.
The build engineer confirms the same failure locally and reports no runner, dependency, compilation, or timeout errors.
state.request: Route the failure to exactly one owner using the supplied rubrics.

reference.reason: Route to the application owner. With `normalizeWhitespace=false`, the stated intent requires preserving the tab, but the patch strips it unconditionally. Repeated CI and local reproduction rule against test flakiness and infrastructure failure.

criteria.false: No — the latest required run contains at least one failure that neither satisfies the flaky exemption nor has a matching base-branch reproduction.
criteria.true: Yes — the latest required run passes, or all its failures satisfy a policy exemption or have a matching base-branch reproduction.

decision.instructions: Readiness decision: Is change 8f31 safe to merge now? Under repository policy, a change is safe only if the latest required run passes, or every failure either qualifies for the stated flaky exemption or is reproduced on the base branch in the same environment. Apply the latest temporal update rather than relying only on the initial run.

state.speaker: Software developer
state.text: Change 8f31 adds null handling to ConfigParser. CI run 441 stopped before tests because the package registry timed out; I think this is infrastructure-only and safe to merge.

state.speaker: Build engineer
state.text: Run 441 is confirmed infrastructure-related. I restarted it on the same Linux image and dependency lockfile as run 442.

state.speaker: Test automation engineer
state.text: Update: run 442 completed the build but ConfigParserTest.rejectsEmptyOverride failed twice. The test passed on 19 of the last 20 base-branch runs; policy grants a flaky exemption only with at least 2 failures in those 20 runs.

state.speaker: Code reviewer
state.text: The run 442 stack trace ends at the line modified by 8f31. No same-environment base-branch reproduction has been recorded.

reference.reason: No. Although run 441 was an infrastructure failure, the later run 442 exposed a relevant test failure at the changed line. With only 1 failure in 20 base runs, the test misses the exemption threshold, and no same-environment base reproduction exists.

criteria.false: No — route the failure to the test, build, or infrastructure owner instead of the application owner.
criteria.true: Yes — route the CI failure to the application owner because the application change reproducibly violates the documented rounding requirement.

decision.instructions: Answer yes if Chen should route the failure to the application owner. Route to application when the changed application behavior reproducibly violates the documented requirement. Route to test only if the expectation conflicts with the requirement, to build if compilation or packaging fails, and to infrastructure if runner or service disruption prevents a valid test result. A recovered warning does not override completed, reproducible test evidence.

input.state: Software developer Mira changed invoice rounding from half-up to floor. In CI, `InvoiceTotalTest.rounds_tax` expected $10.50 but received $10.49 on three runners; a local run at the same commit produced the same assertion. The test passed in the previous 40 builds, and the test code, dependency lockfile, and runner image were unchanged. Mira claims infrastructure caused the failure because the first job logged a transient cache-download timeout. Build engineer Owen notes that the retry succeeded, compilation completed, and all three jobs reached the identical assertion. Test automation engineer Priya confirms the expected value matches the documented half-up requirement. Code reviewer Chen must route the failure.

reference.reason: The application change replaced required half-up rounding with floor rounding, and the resulting $10.49 assertion failure reproduced locally and on three runners. The cache timeout is conflicting evidence but recovered before successful compilation and test execution, so it does not support infrastructure routing.

criteria: 0 — Unverified: Mandatory evidence for the claimed owner is missing, or available evidence leaves a plausible competing owner; do not route or merge on the claim.
1 — Partially verified: All mandatory evidence is present and supports the claimed owner, but at least one material ambiguity remains; route tentatively and require follow-up before merge.
2 — Fully verified: All mandatory evidence is present, directly supports the claimed owner, and rules out material competing causes; route confidently and permit merge on this issue.
decision.instructions: Use the ordered completeness rubric. Missing mandatory evidence controls the result even when other evidence is suggestive. Select exactly one level.

state.context: A software developer asks a code reviewer to merge a parser refactor, claiming its only CI failure belongs to infrastructure. The build engineer normally supplies runner diagnostics, while the test automation engineer tracks test stability.
evidence: Linux job log: unit tests ran successfully until `ParserRecoveryTest` timed out after 60 seconds; no DNS, checkout, container, or compiler errors appear.
The change modifies parser recovery code exercised by the timed-out test.
One manual rerun passed. Test history shows 50 prior runs with no failures.

The runner-health artifact is missing because diagnostics upload was skipped. Repository policy requires that artifact to verify an infrastructure attribution; a passing rerun alone is not sufficient.
state.request: Rate how completely the claimed infrastructure cause is verified for merge routing.

reference.reason: The mandatory runner-health artifact is missing, so policy prevents verification of the infrastructure claim. The changed code also directly affects the timed-out test, and one passing rerun is insufficient.

legend.0: 0 — Unverified: Mandatory evidence for the claimed owner is missing, or available evidence leaves a plausible competing owner; do not route or merge on the claim.
legend.1: 1 — Partially verified: All mandatory evidence is present and supports the claimed owner, but at least one material ambiguity remains; route tentatively and require follow-up before merge.
legend.2: 2 — Fully verified: All mandatory evidence is present, directly supports the claimed owner, and rules out material competing causes; route confidently and permit merge on this issue.

criteria: Not ready: an in-scope failure exists and the known-flake exception is unavailable, so code changes or failure diagnosis are required before merging.
Conditionally ready: an in-scope failure exists, but the known-flake exception applies; one clean rerun is required before merging.
Ready now: all in-scope required tests passed, or every failure is outside the affected scope, so no rerun or remediation is required.
decision.instructions: Determine the PR's current merge-readiness level under the stated scope rule and known-flake exception.

state.speaker: Software developer
state.text: PR 482 changes only ParserCache internals; public interfaces and dependency files are unchanged. Linux parser unit tests passed, but Windows cli_integration timed out after 120 seconds.

state.speaker: Test automation engineer
state.text: The CLI consumes ParserCache, so cli_integration is in scope. The identical Windows timeout occurred on main in 3 of the last 80 runs and passed on immediate rerun each time. This run contains no assertion failure.

state.speaker: Build engineer
state.text: The agent had 41% free disk, stable network, and no runner warnings. Compilation and environment setup completed normally.

state.speaker: Code reviewer
state.text: Policy: an in-scope failure blocks merging unless the known-flake exception applies. That exception permits conditional merging after one clean rerun when the same non-assertion signature previously occurred on main; it never applies after a public-interface change.

reference.reason: The failed CLI test is in scope, so the PR is not fully ready. However, the timeout matches a documented main-branch flake, has no assertion or infrastructure evidence, and no public interface changed; therefore the exception allows a clean-rerun path to merging.

legend.0: Not ready: an in-scope failure exists and the known-flake exception is unavailable, so code changes or failure diagnosis are required before merging.
legend.1: Conditionally ready: an in-scope failure exists, but the known-flake exception applies; one clean rerun is required before merging.
legend.2: Ready now: all in-scope required tests passed, or every failure is outside the affected scope, so no rerun or remediation is required.

criteria.catalog_confirmed_incident: Confirm a real incident and route to Catalog when both alert thresholds are met, the first slow server span is in Catalog, and dependencies are healthy.
criteria.database_dependency: Route to the database team only when the shared database is degraded and trace latency originates in database subspans.
criteria.none_of_above: Use only if the evidence is contradictory or does not satisfy any of the four explicit rubrics.
criteria.search_rollback: Route to Search and request rollback only when the affected region has search_v2 exposure above 20% and latency rose after its deployment.
criteria.suppress_nonincident: Suppress the alert only when p95 or error-rate evidence fails to satisfy the runbook’s incident threshold.

decision.instructions: Apply the stated incident threshold and conditional routing rules. Select exactly one option; deployment timing alone does not override the deployment record’s rollback condition.

state.context: At 14:20 UTC, an on-call engineer assesses a ShopFront product-page alert in us-east-1. The runbook confirms an incident when p95 exceeds 800 ms for 10 minutes and errors exceed 2%.
evidence: Metrics show p95 of 1.4 seconds for 14 minutes and a 3.1% error rate.
In 40 sampled traces, 34 have their first slow server span inside Catalog API; its database subspans remain normal.
The dependency dashboard reports Search and the shared database healthy in every region.
Search deployed at 14:05. Its record says to roll back only if latency rises where search_v2 exposure exceeds 20%; exposure in us-east-1 is 0%.
Routing rule: route to the service containing the first slow server span unless its dependency is degraded; suppress only when incident thresholds are unmet.
state.request: Choose the correct incident assessment and primary routing destination.

reference.reason: The alert meets both incident thresholds. Catalog API is the first slow server span in 34 of 40 traces, while its dependencies are healthy. The Search rollback condition is false because search_v2 exposure is 0%, so this is a confirmed incident routed to Catalog.

criteria.noise: Classify as Noise because the latest user-visible error rate is below 1%.
criteria.none_of_above: Choose None of the above because the supplied evidence cannot be classified under the stated rubric.
criteria.observe: Classify as Observe because at least 1% errors are present but fewer than 10 consecutive complete buckets exist.
criteria.sev1: Classify as SEV-1 because at least 10 consecutive complete buckets are at least 20%.
criteria.sev2: Classify as SEV-2 because at least 10 consecutive complete buckets are at least 5% but below 20%.
criteria.sev3: Classify as SEV-3 because at least 10 consecutive complete buckets are at least 1% but below 5%.

decision.instructions: Rate the alert under this exhaustive rubric: Noise if the latest rate is below 1%; Observe if it is at least 1% but fewer than 10 consecutive complete buckets exist; SEV-3 if 10 or more consecutive buckets are at least 1% but below 5%; SEV-2 if 10 or more are at least 5% but below 20%; SEV-1 if 10 or more are at least 20%; choose None of the above only if the supplied evidence cannot fit any rubric.

state.speaker: On-call engineer
state.text: At 14:08, checkout-api has six complete one-minute buckets since 14:02 with user-visible HTTP 5xx rates of 5.0–5.4%. The alert requires assessment; traffic is normal.

state.speaker: Site reliability engineer
state.text: Traces attribute 96% of failures to checkout-api’s own tax-rounding handler. Payment and database dependencies report healthy status in both regions.

state.speaker: Service owner
state.text: The only deployment was a catalog-ui release at 13:40. checkout-api has had no deployment or configuration change today.

state.speaker: Incident coordinator
state.text: At 14:12, four additional complete buckets, through 14:11, show 5.0–5.2% errors. Runbook: classify using consecutive complete buckets; a value exactly on a boundary enters the higher severity band.

reference.reason: The temporal update raises the evidence from six to exactly ten consecutive complete buckets, all at least 5.0% and below 20%. The boundary rule places exactly 5.0% in the higher band, so this is SEV-2.

criteria.false: No — do not route the alert to the Catalog service owner; route it to the Pricing service owner.
criteria.true: Yes — route the alert to the Catalog service owner.

decision.instructions: Decide whether the alert should be routed to the Catalog service owner under the supplied runbook.

input.state: The site reliability engineer reviews a Catalog API alert showing 11% HTTP 500s for six minutes. A Catalog deployment finished eight minutes earlier, suggesting Catalog ownership. However, 18 sampled traces show Catalog succeeding until calls to Pricing time out, and Pricing connection-pool saturation reached 97% during the same period. Pricing’s status panel still reports healthy. The runbook says to route an alert to the service with the earliest failing span when at least three traces and one independent metric agree; deployment timing alone is insufficient to establish ownership. Under this rule, the earliest supported failure is Pricing.

reference.reason: No. Although the recent Catalog deployment and API-level alert suggest Catalog, 18 traces identify Pricing as the earliest failing span and Pricing saturation independently corroborates it. The runbook therefore routes ownership to Pricing; its healthy status panel is outweighed by the required evidence.

criteria.false: The alert is routed to the Payments service owner because at least one runbook condition conclusively identifies or confirms Payments degradation.
criteria.true: The alert remains with the site reliability engineer because the evidence does not satisfy either condition required to route it to Payments.

decision.instructions: Answer yes or no using only the stated routing runbook and evidence. Missing required routing evidence must be treated as unavailable, not inferred.

state.context: An on-call engineer is assessing a fictional ShopWave production alert. The routing runbook says to assign an alert to the Payments service owner only when a completed trace identifies Payments as the slow component or the dependency dashboard confirms Payments degradation. Otherwise, the site reliability engineer retains the alert for investigation.
evidence: Checkout API p95 latency rose from 280 ms to 1.9 s for eight minutes; 4% of requests exceeded the two-second objective.
The sampled trace ends at the Checkout-to-Payments call because downstream spans are missing.
The Payments dependency dashboard has no data for the relevant interval.
Deployment records show no Checkout or Payments releases within six hours.
state.request: Should the site reliability engineer retain the alert rather than route it to the Payments service owner?

reference.reason: Yes. Although Checkout latency is elevated, neither required basis for Payments routing is available: the trace lacks downstream spans, and the Payments dependency dashboard has no data. The runbook therefore assigns continued investigation to the site reliability engineer.

criteria: 0 — No verified production impact: only excluded synthetic or beta traffic is affected, or in-scope production failures remain below 1% in every region during the window.
1 — Minor verified impact: at least 1% but less than 5% of in-scope production requests fail in one region for 10 minutes, with no other region at 1% or higher.
2 — Significant regional impact: at least 5% but less than 25% of in-scope production requests fail in exactly one region for at least 10 minutes; escalate to the owning service team.
3 — Major broad impact: at least 25% of in-scope production requests fail in any region for at least 10 minutes, or at least 5% fail in two or more regions for that duration.
decision.instructions: Assign the alert an impact level using the ordered rubric. Assess only the stated 10-minute window and apply the runbook’s scope and exceptions.

state.speaker: On-call engineer
state.text: Checkout API alert: from 14:20–14:30 UTC, exactly 5.0% of production customer requests in eu-west returned HTTP 503; 2,000 requests were sampled. US and APAC remained below 0.2%.

state.speaker: Site reliability engineer
state.text: The dashboard already excludes synthetic probes and the beta tenant. Traces from 14 affected customer requests end at Checkout’s pricing adapter, while Pricing itself reports healthy.

state.speaker: Service owner
state.text: Checkout release 8.4.1 reached eu-west at 14:18; no other region received it. Rollback has not started.

state.speaker: Incident coordinator
state.text: Runbook: use production customer traffic only. Synthetic and beta traffic never count. A threshold written “at least” is inclusive; regional incidents meeting it are escalated to the service owner.

reference.reason: After excluded synthetic and beta traffic is removed, exactly 5.0% of in-scope production customer requests failed in one region for exactly 10 minutes. The inclusive boundary satisfies level 2, while healthy US and APAC traffic prevents level 3.

legend.0: 0 — No verified production impact: only excluded synthetic or beta traffic is affected, or in-scope production failures remain below 1% in every region during the window.
legend.1: 1 — Minor verified impact: at least 1% but less than 5% of in-scope production requests fail in one region for 10 minutes, with no other region at 1% or higher.
legend.2: 2 — Significant regional impact: at least 5% but less than 25% of in-scope production requests fail in exactly one region for at least 10 minutes; escalate to the owning service team.
legend.3: 3 — Major broad impact: at least 25% of in-scope production requests fail in any region for at least 10 minutes, or at least 5% fail in two or more regions for that duration.

criteria: 0 — No incident: the alert is false or expected, customer-facing error rates remain at baseline, and completed purchases are unaffected.
1 — Minor operational issue: a real fault exists, but it is confined to internal processing or affects fewer than 5% of customer requests without blocking purchases.

2 — Moderate user impact: 5% to 20% of customer requests fail, or purchases are degraded but customers have a confirmed workaround; service-team response is required without major-incident escalation.

3 — Major user impact: more than 20% of customer-facing requests fail and purchases are blocked without a workaround; notify the incident coordinator and immediately escalate to the responsible service or dependency team.
decision.instructions: Assess the alert's user-impact level using the evidence and runbook. Select exactly one ordered level, resolving references such as “the former” and “the latter” to the named services.

input.state: At 14:20 UTC, the on-call engineer receives a Checkout API alert: HTTP 503 responses rose from 0.3% to 42% for 14 minutes, and completed purchases fell 38%. Traces list Checkout API and PaymentGateway: the former returned 503 after the latter timed out. No Checkout deployment occurred today; its last release was three days ago. Dependency status reports PaymentGateway latency above 12 seconds, while all other dependencies are healthy. The service owner confirms there is no payment workaround. The runbook says a customer-facing failure rate above 20% with blocked purchases is a major incident requiring the incident coordinator and immediate dependency-team escalation.

reference.reason: “The former” refers to Checkout API, so the 503s are customer-facing; “the latter” identifies PaymentGateway as the failing dependency. Checkout failures are 42%, purchases are blocked with no workaround, and the runbook requires major-incident escalation above 20%.

legend.0: 0 — No incident: the alert is false or expected, customer-facing error rates remain at baseline, and completed purchases are unaffected.
legend.1: 1 — Minor operational issue: a real fault exists, but it is confined to internal processing or affects fewer than 5% of customer requests without blocking purchases.
legend.2: 2 — Moderate user impact: 5% to 20% of customer requests fail, or purchases are degraded but customers have a confirmed workaround; service-team response is required without major-incident escalation.
legend.3: 3 — Major user impact: more than 20% of customer-facing requests fail and purchases are blocked without a workaround; notify the incident coordinator and immediately escalate to the responsible service or dependency team.

criteria.accept_batch: Accept when no earlier disposition applies: completeness is at least 98.0%, duplicates are at most 1.0%, schema errors are at most 0.1%, and transformations are supported.
criteria.conditional_rework: Fifth precedence: return for remediation if earlier conditions do not apply and completeness is at least 95.0% but below 98.0%.
criteria.duplicate_quarantine: Second precedence: quarantine if no pipeline-integrity hold applies and the duplicate rate exceeds 1.0%.
criteria.pipeline_integrity_hold: First precedence: hold and route to the data engineer if any unsupported coercion exists, or if the newest report is incomplete or does not match the immutable batch hash.
criteria.product_schema_hold: Third precedence: hold for the product-data owner if neither earlier condition applies and schema errors exceed 0.1%.
criteria.source_repair_required: Fourth precedence: route to the source-system operator if earlier conditions do not apply and required-field completeness is below 95.0%.

decision.instructions: Choose the batch-readiness disposition. Apply the option rubrics in their stated precedence order; threshold equality passes. Only a completed temporal update for the identical batch hash may replace earlier evidence.

state.speaker: Data quality analyst
state.text: At 13:40, validation for batch C-184 (SHA-256 ending 91bf) reported 8,000 customer rows: consent_timestamp completeness 95.1%, duplicate rate 0.9%, and schema-error rate 0.0%.

state.speaker: Data engineer
state.text: The pipeline had mistakenly validated before the approved UTC conversion finished. I reran that step without changing source values or row count; the transformation audit shows no coercions or fabricated timestamps.

state.speaker: Source-system operator
state.text: The completed 14:20 report covers the same 91bf batch hash: completeness is now exactly 98.0%, duplicates remain 0.9%, and schema errors remain 0.0%.

state.speaker: Application administrator
state.text: Policy says a later completed report supersedes an earlier report only for the same immutable hash. Apply dispositions in listed precedence. Acceptance requires completeness at least 98.0%, duplicates at most 1.0%, schema errors at most 0.1%, and no unsupported transformation.

reference.reason: The 14:20 completed update is eligible because it covers the same immutable hash. Its 98.0% completeness is exactly passing, while 0.9% duplicates and 0.0% schema errors are within limits, and the audit found no unsupported transformation.

criteria.accept_batch: Accept V-204 only if all applicable validation and duplicate reports agree that the normalized vendor_id field has no collisions.
criteria.none_of_above: Use when conflicting or untraceable evidence prevents both acceptance and a supported pipeline-owner route.
criteria.route_pipeline_owner: Hold V-204 and route it to the pipeline owner only if normalized-ID collisions are confirmed in the current V-204 run.

decision.instructions: Choose the readiness decision whose rubric is fully supported by the evidence. If neither substantive rubric is satisfied, choose none_of_above.

input.state: Data quality analyst Mira reviews batch V-204 of 50,000 vendor records. The schema requires vendor_id to be unique after the pipeline applies trim-and-uppercase normalization. The validator summary for run V-204 reports zero duplicate vendor_ids and marks the batch ready. However, a duplicate report lists 18 normalized-ID collisions, including raw values “ab-17 ” and “AB-17”. That report has no run ID or generation timestamp, so it cannot be tied to V-204. Policy permits acceptance only when all applicable reports agree, and permits routing to the pipeline owner only when a collision is confirmed in the current run.

reference.reason: The validator supports acceptance, but the unidentified duplicate report conflicts with it, so the required report agreement is absent. The collisions also cannot be confirmed as belonging to the current run, so pipeline routing is unsupported.

criteria.false: No — do not mark the batch ready because at least one threshold is unmet or required acceptance evidence is missing.
criteria.true: Yes — mark the batch ready because all acceptance thresholds and mandatory evidence requirements are demonstrated.

decision.instructions: Answer yes only if every stated acceptance condition is supported by the supplied evidence. If required evidence is missing, answer no even when available metrics appear to pass.

state.context: Data quality analyst Mira is reviewing customer batch CUS-184 for the fictional Northstar CRM. Policy permits acceptance only when post-transformation critical-field completeness is at least 99.5%, duplicate rate is below 0.5%, and an input-to-output row reconciliation is supplied.
evidence: Source-system operator reports 20,000 input rows and 99.8% pre-transformation completeness for customer_id and email.
Duplicate report identifies 60 duplicate rows, a 0.3% rate.
Transformation rules tell the data engineer to replace syntactically invalid emails with null.
The validation package contains no post-transformation completeness results and no reconciliation showing transformed, rejected, and loaded row counts.
Application administrator confirms both missing reports are mandatory acceptance evidence.
state.request: Should Mira mark CUS-184 ready for acceptance now?

reference.reason: The duplicate rate passes, but only pre-transformation completeness is reported. Because transformations can null invalid emails, post-transformation completeness is unknown, and the mandatory row reconciliation is also missing. Readiness is therefore unsupported.

criteria.false: Reject batch B-142 because at least one acceptance requirement is not satisfied.
criteria.true: Accept batch B-142 because it satisfies all acceptance requirements after applying the documented scope exception.

decision.instructions: Decide whether the batch meets the stated acceptance rubric. Answer yes only if both the duplicate and scoped completeness requirements are satisfied.

state.speaker: Data engineer
state.text: Batch B-142 contains 10,000 customer records. Schema requires customer_id and ship_country. The approved transformation keeps the newest updated_at record for duplicate customer_id values; the duplicate report shows 12 before transformation and zero afterward.

state.speaker: Data quality analyst
state.text: Acceptance requires zero post-transformation duplicate IDs and at least 99.95% ship_country completeness among in-scope records. Records tagged import_mode=history are exempt because they are archived and excluded from product search.

state.speaker: Source-system operator
state.text: The exception report identifies 80 history records. Five of those lack ship_country. I verified that all 80 carry the history tag in the source export.

state.speaker: Application administrator
state.text: The validation summary reports seven missing ship_country values total: five exempt history records and two active records. No other schema errors remain. Should B-142 be accepted?

reference.reason: Yes. Post-transformation duplicates are zero. Excluding the 80 verified history exceptions leaves 9,920 in-scope records, with 9,918 complete: 99.9798%, which exceeds 99.95%. The exception is decisive because counting all seven missing values would yield only 99.93%.

criteria: 0 — Post-transformation completeness is below 90%.
1 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 90% but below 95%.
2 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 95% but below 98%.
3 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 98% but below 99.5%.
4 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 99.5%.
decision.instructions: Calculate the percentage of required cells populated after applying the stated transformation rule, then select the matching completeness level.

input.state: A data quality analyst reviews a 100-record customer batch supplied by the source-system operator. The product schema requires customer_name, email, and region_code, giving 300 required cells. The validation summary reports 12 blanks: six region_code, three email, and three customer_name. The data engineer’s rule states, “If region_code is blank and postal_country is present, derive region_code from postal_country; after derivation, it counts as populated.” In all six affected records, it is present; sample records confirm values such as CA and DE. The duplicate report finds no duplicates. The application administrator requests the post-transformation completeness rating.

reference.reason: “It” refers to postal_country, so all six blank region_code cells can be derived and counted as populated. That leaves six unresolved blanks among 300 required cells: 294/300 = 98%, which is level 3.

legend.0: 0 — Post-transformation completeness is below 90%.
legend.1: 1 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 90% but below 95%.
legend.2: 2 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 95% but below 98%.
legend.3: 3 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 98% but below 99.5%.
legend.4: 4 — Post-transformation completeness is at least 99.5%.

criteria: Accept: No schema violations, conflicting required identifiers, unexplained record loss, or material transformation defects are evidenced.
Accept with monitoring: Only reversible, non-key formatting differences affect at most 1% of rows, and documented normalization preserves the values.
Conditional hold for application administrator: Valid source keys are intact, but product-owned mappings, allowed values, or display rules remain unresolved for at most 1% of rows.
Hold for data engineer: The source extract conforms to schema, but pipeline logic creates duplicates, drops records, or changes key values; rerun after pipeline correction.

Reject and route to source-system operator: At least 1% of rows contain conflicting required identifiers attributable to the source, and the configured import would overwrite identities or otherwise cause irreversible ambiguity; require a corrected extract before import.
decision.instructions: Choose exactly one ordered readiness level. Apply the concrete thresholds below, distinguish schema-threatening evidence from harmless formatting facts, and do not rely solely on the validation summary’s recommendation.

state.context: Data quality analyst Mara reviews a 50,000-row Northstar CRM customer batch before the application administrator schedules production import.
evidence: Schema requires external_customer_id to be non-null and unique; account_status must be active or inactive.
Validation summary reports all required fields valid and recommends acceptance.
Duplicate report finds 1,240 rows sharing external IDs with different legal_name values; configured upsert is last-row-wins.
Sample records confirm three such conflicting pairs.
Source-system operator attributes them to a replay window and can re-extract; data engineer confirms the pipeline followed configuration.
Seventy-one emails are uppercase but normalized; 18 postal codes lack hyphens, which the application administrator says display correctly.
state.request: Score batch-import readiness and identify the action and owner prescribed by the selected level.

reference.reason: Level 4 applies because 1,240 of 50,000 rows (2.48%) have conflicting required unique IDs, exceeding the 1% threshold, and last-row-wins would silently overwrite customer identities. The source-system operator confirmed replay corruption and can re-extract. Uppercase emails and postal-code formatting are distractors because normalization or display support resolves them.

legend.0: Accept: No schema violations, conflicting required identifiers, unexplained record loss, or material transformation defects are evidenced.
legend.1: Accept with monitoring: Only reversible, non-key formatting differences affect at most 1% of rows, and documented normalization preserves the values.
legend.2: Conditional hold for application administrator: Valid source keys are intact, but product-owned mappings, allowed values, or display rules remain unresolved for at most 1% of rows.
legend.3: Hold for data engineer: The source extract conforms to schema, but pipeline logic creates duplicates, drops records, or changes key values; rerun after pipeline correction.
legend.4: Reject and route to source-system operator: At least 1% of rows contain conflicting required identifiers attributable to the source, and the configured import would overwrite identities or otherwise cause irreversible ambiguity; require a corrected extract before import.

criteria.none_of_above: The release is not ready and its failed gates span multiple owners, or the evidence cannot support either substantive classification.
criteria.release_ready: Every required defect, compatibility, installation, signing, and rollback gate passes under the authoritative evidence.
criteria.single_owner_blocked: At least one release gate fails, and all failed gates belong exclusively to one owner: development, compatibility, packaging, or release operations.

decision.instructions: Classify release readiness using the supplied policy and evidence. Select “release_ready” only if every gate passes. Select “single_owner_blocked” only if the release fails but every failed gate belongs to one owner. Otherwise select “none_of_above.”

input.state: For fictional desktop app Northstar Notes 6.2 RC3, the release manager’s dashboard says “Ready: all gates green.” However, the desktop developer’s signed defect list shows open Sev-2 DN-418: exporting an encrypted notebook crashes. The compatibility tester’s signed report passes all required Windows 11 and macOS 15 checks. The deployment specialist’s signed packaging report confirms valid signatures and clean installs, but rollback leaves the updater service disabled. Policy requires no open Sev-1/Sev-2 defects and successful install and rollback. Signed detailed reports override dashboard summaries. A failed defect gate belongs to development; a failed rollback gate belongs to packaging.

reference.reason: The dashboard’s readiness claim is overridden by the signed reports. RC3 fails both the development-owned defect gate due to open Sev-2 DN-418 and the packaging-owned rollback gate because the updater service is disabled. It is neither ready nor blocked by a single owner.

criteria.A — Pass the release gate: Choose only when every supported platform has all required recorded checks and no blocking defect or failed gate remains.
criteria.B — Fail and route to desktop developmen: Choose only when evidence records a product-code failure or an open blocking defect requiring a developer fix.
criteria.C — Hold as undetermined; request ARM64: Choose when a supported platform lacks mandatory packaging or installation evidence; ask the deployment specialist to run and record the missing checks.
criteria.D — Fail and remove ARM64 from documenta: Choose only when ARM64 has a recorded incompatibility and an approved scope change requires the compatibility tester and release manager to remove it from the support matrix.

decision.instructions: Select exactly one option. Apply the gate policy literally: distinguish a recorded failure from missing mandatory evidence and route evidence collection to the role that owns installers.

state.context: The release manager is assessing fictional note-taking desktop app QuillDesk 8.2 RC3. The desktop developer reports the synchronization fix complete, the compatibility tester owns platform checks, and the deployment specialist owns installers and rollback validation.
evidence: Regression suite: 1,248 passed, 0 failed; no open severity-1 or severity-2 defects.
Compatibility passed on Windows 11 x64, macOS 15 Intel, and macOS 15 Apple silicon.
Packaging reports show valid signatures and clean installs for all tested platforms, but contain no Windows 11 ARM64 result.

The support matrix includes Windows 11 ARM64. Gate policy requires a recorded install, launch, uninstall, and signature check for every supported platform. Missing mandatory evidence means readiness is undetermined, not failed. Rollback rehearsal passed.
state.request: Under the stated gate policy, determine RC3 readiness and the proper next action.

reference.reason: Windows 11 ARM64 is supported, but its mandatory installation and signature results are missing. The policy therefore makes readiness undetermined, and installer evidence belongs to the deployment specialist.
reference.target: C — Hold as undetermined; request ARM64 evidence from deployment

decision.choice: C — Hold as undetermined; request ARM64 evidence from deployment

criteria.false: No — do not approve it now because at least one applicable release gate fails.
criteria.true: Yes — approve the release candidate now because every applicable release gate passes.

decision.instructions: Readiness verification: decide whether the release candidate passes the stated approval gate now. Apply the scope and exception rule exactly as written.

state.speaker: Release manager
state.text: Gate rule: approve only if all in-scope platforms pass, no in-scope Severity-1/2 defects remain, installers are signed, and rollback is rehearsed. Windows 10 failures may be excepted only after release notes explicitly mark Windows 10 unsupported.

state.speaker: Compatibility tester
state.text: Windows 11 23H2 and macOS 15 passed. Windows 10 22H2 crashes when importing profiles; defect DESK-418 is open at Severity 2. Linux is outside this release’s scope.

state.speaker: Deployment specialist
state.text: Both installers are signed and clean. The rollback rehearsal restored version 8.4 and user settings successfully.

state.speaker: Desktop developer
state.text: The candidate is stable on supported systems. I requested removal of Windows 10 support, but documentation has not yet added the unsupported-platform notice.

reference.reason: No. Windows 10 remains in scope because its exception is not effective until the release notes mark it unsupported. Therefore, open Severity-2 defect DESK-418 blocks approval despite the other gates passing.

criteria.false: No — route the blocker to another team because it does not concern installer construction or signing.
criteria.true: Yes — route the blocker to packaging because it concerns installer construction or signing.

decision.instructions: Decide whether the blocker described by the deployment specialist should be routed to packaging under the stated policy.

input.state: For Northstar Notes 4.2 RC3, the release manager reviews 186 passing functional tests and one open blocker. The desktop developer confirms the application binaries run without crashes. The compatibility tester reports passes on Windows 11, macOS 15, and Ubuntu 24.04. The deployment specialist finds that the Windows installer omitted the required signature from the updater executable; she says it triggers an administrator warning. The packaging report reproduces this omission, while the rollback plan successfully restores 4.1. Policy routes installer construction or signing defects to packaging, application-runtime defects to development, compatibility failures to testing, and rollback failures to release operations. Any open blocker fails the release gate.

reference.reason: Yes. “It” refers to the unsigned updater executable, and the reproduced omission is an installer-signing defect, which policy explicitly routes to packaging.

criteria: Not ready — at least one mandatory release gate fails or a release-blocking defect remains open; route the blocking issue to the responsible team before release.
Conditionally ready — every mandatory technical gate passes and no release blocker is open, but a documented nonblocking issue still requires an approved waiver or release-note action.
Ready — every mandatory gate passes, no release-blocking defect is open, packages are signed, and any nonblocking documentation work is already resolved or approved for shipment.

input.state: A park visitor reports an irrigation leak beside Cedar Park’s east gate at path marker E-4. The attached time-stamped photo shows water spraying from a broken sprinkler valve and pooling across the full width of the paved accessible path; the visible E-4 marker and east-gate sign match the report. Park policy routes confirmed irrigation faults to the field repair technician. Priority P1 covers immediate life-threatening hazards; P2 covers active slip hazards or fully blocked accessible paths; P3 covers nonhazardous damage. A path segment is temporarily closed only when matching photo and location evidence confirms a current obstruction or hazard. The grounds maintenance dispatcher proposes routing the issue to the field repair technician, closing the E-4 segment, and assigning P2.

reference.reason: Yes. The photo and visible location markers explicitly match the report and confirm both an irrigation fault and water covering the accessible path. Policy therefore supports routing to the field repair technician, temporarily closing the hazardous segment, and assigning P2 rather than P1 or P3.

decision.instructions: Choose exactly one level. Rate verified support for maintenance action, not the seriousness of the visitor’s original allegation. The levels are ordered from lowest to highest support.

criteria.deny_low: Do not release: LOW confidence because the route is incorrect or material facts conflict with the intake record.
criteria.hold_medium: Send to the Transit Depot Vault but hold the backpack: MEDIUM confidence because an identifying requirement is missing or custody is incomplete.
criteria.release_high: Send to the Transit Depot Vault and release to Mara: HIGH confidence because custody is intact and both required identifying elements match without material conflict.

decision.instructions: Apply this rubric: HIGH—route is correct, custody is intact, and the claimant supplies both a unique identifier and one undisclosed feature without a material conflict; release is permitted. MEDIUM—route is correct and the claim is plausible, but either required identifying element is missing or custody has a gap; hold for more evidence. LOW—route is wrong or a material item, date, location, or identifier conflicts; do not release. Weather, staff clothing, and similar incidental observations are distractors, not material conflicts.

state.context: A navy canvas backpack was found on Route 18 bus 604 at 18:20 on 12 May. Transit operator Imani Cole sealed it as T-884 and delivered it to the civic hall receptionist, who transferred the unbroken seal to lost-property custodian Arun Vale.
evidence: The intake record lists serial patch BP-77104 and a brass key inside a torn inner-lining pocket; neither detail was publicly disclosed.
Claimant Mara Venn reported losing it on Route 18 around 18:00 and provided BP-77104 and the hidden key detail.
Mara also recalled heavy rain and said the receptionist wore a red scarf. The custody record does not mention weather or clothing.
Policy routes property found in transit vehicles to the Transit Depot Vault, regardless of where it was handed in.
state.request: Choose the proper route and determine whether Mara's evidence permits release under the confidence rubric.

reference.reason: Transit-vehicle property goes to the Transit Depot Vault. Seal T-884 remained intact, and Mara supplied both the exact serial BP-77104 and the undisclosed hidden-key detail. Her date, time, and route are consistent; rain and scarf details are immaterial distractors.

criteria.level_1_insufficient_reject: Reject or investigate with Level 1 confidence: location/date requirements fail, no sufficient private detail matches, or a material contradiction exists.
criteria.level_2_partial_hold: Hold with Level 2 confidence: location and date match, but only one nonpublic detail matches.
criteria.level_3_strong_release: Release with Level 3 confidence: location and date match, at least two nonpublic details match, and there is no material contradiction.
criteria.level_4_exact_release: Release with Level 4 confidence: a pre-loss unique identifier and at least two nonpublic details match.

decision.instructions: Choose the match-confidence and release decision. Apply this ordered rubric: Level 4 requires a claimant-provided unique identifier created or known before loss plus at least two nonpublic details; Level 3 requires matching location/date plus at least two nonpublic details and no contradiction; Level 2 requires matching location/date but only one nonpublic detail; Level 1 applies when those conditions fail or a material contradiction exists. Semantically equivalent paraphrases count as matching details. Release is allowed only at Levels 3-4.

state.text: On September 12, I found a scarlet canvas tote under a seat on Route 8 and sealed it as T-447 before transferring it to the transit lost-property room.

The mint-green thermos is one nonpublic detail, and the claimant’s wording about J encouraging Mira to take the harder path is a valid paraphrase of the inscription, providing the second. There is no contradiction, but T-447 was an intake code rather than a claimant-provided pre-loss identifier, so Level 4 is not met.

criteria: No release: the claimant has withdrawn the claim or an explicit condition of the claimant’s intent is false, regardless of descriptive matches.
Hold—weak match: intent to claim is active, but evidence consists only of generic features or lacks a custody-compatible date, location, or distinguishing detail.
Hold—strong match: intent is active and the description matches the custody record plus at least one nonpublic distinguishing identifier, but a required verification step remains.

Release authorized: intent is active, custody is consistent, all required checks are complete, and at least two specific identifying details—including one nonpublic detail—match without contradiction.
decision.instructions: Assign the release-readiness level under this policy: a claimant’s explicit conditional intent controls even when item details otherwise match. criteria.complete_immediate_digital_retrieval: The request is complete and correctly routed, and an existing indexed electronic copy can be retrieved immediately without physical archive work.
criteria.complete_manual_archive_retrieval: The archived material is uniquely identifiable, format and delivery are supplied, routing is correct, and staff must retrieve or scan a physical record manually.

decision.instructions: Assign the request’s processing status. Apply these ordered rubrics: a paraphrased subject counts as matching reference information only when the index confirms a unique semantic match. A request is identifiable with either a notice number or two matching references among date, issuing department, facility, and subject. It is complete only if it also specifies copy format and delivery method. Archived paper requiring box retrieval is manual retrieval; an existing indexed electronic file is immediate retrieval.
